content: 1. Since 2015, an increasing number of women have gained access to antiretroviral drugs (ARVs) during pregnancy and breastfeeding. This access is crucial for their own health and for reducing the risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV. For instance, in 2012, approximately 75% of HIV-infected pregnant women received ARVs, which is 400,000 more women compared to 2009. This expanded coverage, along with newer ARV regimens, has significantly reduced mother-to-child HIV transmission rates. 2. However, in many countries with high HIV prevalence, more than half of the children newly infected with HIV acquire the virus during the breastfeeding period. The World Health Organization (WHO), UNAIDS, UNFPA, and UNICEF last revised their guidelines on HIV and infant feeding in 2010. For the first time, these guidelines recommended the use of ARVs to prevent HIV transmission through breastfeeding. 3. Since 2010, WHO has updated its recommendations on ARVs for treating HIV-infected adults and children, as well as for preventing mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT). While the 2013 updates modified ARV regimens to reduce peripartum transmission, the public health and programmatic implications were not fully incorporated into recommendations for infant and young child feeding in high HIV prevalence countries. 4. Implementing global recommendations on HIV and infant feeding at the national level is influenced by several factors. First, countries must adopt these global recommendations into their national frameworks, including allocating budgets for training, implementation, and monitoring. Second, healthcare workers need to trust the recommendations and have the necessary time and resources to integrate them into routine practice. Finally, mothers and communities must understand and value the interventions to accept and adhere to them. 5. In 2012, UNICEF collected data on the implementation of the 2010 global guidelines to better understand the situation, improve technical assistance, and inform advocacy and resource mobilization. The 2010 guidelines on HIV and infant feeding were scheduled for an update in 2015 using the GRADE process outlined by the WHO Guideline Review Committee. 6. To prepare for this update, the WHO Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health (MCA), in collaboration with UNICEF, evaluated the experiences and challenges related to implementing the 2010 guidelines. This evaluation involved three key groups: national ministries of health (MoH) representatives, implementing partners, and networks of HIV-infected mothers. The evaluation was conducted through interviews and an online survey to summarize progress in 22 UNAIDS priority countries (primarily in sub-Saharan Africa and India) and identify key programmatic questions for the Guideline Development Group. 7. The evaluation aimed to assess the quality and extent of the implementation of the 2010 global guidelines on HIV and infant feeding in the 22 countries included in the UNAIDS Global Plan. The findings were intended to inform future guideline updates. 8. The primary objectives of the evaluation were to: Collect, compile, and analyze information on HIV and infant feeding policies in the 22 countries. Assess the quality and extent of national policy implementation on HIV and infant feeding in these countries. Document challenges faced by countries in implementing these policies. Identify aspects of the 2010 global guidelines for potential review. Provide suggestions for areas to consider in the upcoming review of WHO recommendations. 9. Secondary objectives included: Evaluating each country’s progress in implementing recommended interventions for HIV and infant feeding. Gathering information on capacity-building and training conducted on these interventions. Collecting national data and tools for monitoring and evaluating infant feeding practices among HIV-infected mothers and interventions to prevent postpartum HIV transmission. 10. The evaluation used a combination of semi-structured phone interviews and electronic surveys. The interviews targeted national representatives responsible for HIV and infant feeding, while the surveys were directed at implementing partners and organizations involved in HIV-related programs. 11. The study population included: National MoH representatives, including managers responsible for PMTCT and infant and young child feeding (IYCF) programs. Representatives of organizations implementing HIV-related programs and supporting HIV and infant feeding initiatives. 12. All 22 countries included in the UNAIDS Global Plan were invited to participate in the evaluation. These countries included Angola, Burundi, Botswana, Cameroon, Chad, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Ghana, India, Ivory Coast, Kenya, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, Nigeria, South Africa, Swaziland, Uganda, Tanzania, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. 13. Ethical considerations were addressed throughout the evaluation. Consent was obtained from participants before interviews and at the beginning of the online survey. The data collected were not anonymous, as the identity and role of respondents were known to the interviewers. However, no personal information beyond professional capacity was collected, and all identifiers were removed during analysis and reporting. 14. The evaluation faced limitations, including the inability to interview mothers, healthcare workers, or community members directly involved in infant feeding practices. Observations of practices at health facilities and homes were also not possible. Additionally, there was a risk of non-responses or incomplete questionnaires, particularly for the online survey, which could limit the accuracy and detail of the information collected. 15. Despite these challenges, the evaluation collected data from 21 of the 22 invited countries between December 2014 and September 2015. Interviews with MoH representatives lasted between one and two and a half hours, excluding preparation time. The results summarized the progress made by these countries and identified key programmatic questions for the upcoming review of the 2010 global guidelines on HIV and infant feeding.
